subject: chemistry
title: Electrolysis and the Faraday constant
key_idea: In electrolysis, the products depend on the state of the electrolyte, the electrode potentials and the concentration. The charge passed is Q = It. Dividing by the Faraday constant gives the moles of electrons, and the half-equation links them to the amount of product.

blocks.text: Electrolysis uses an electric current to drive a non-spontaneous reaction. This section covers how to predict what forms at each electrode.

items: Positive ions (cations) move to the cathode, where they gain electrons. Reduction happens there.
Negative ions (anions) move to the anode, where they lose electrons. Oxidation happens there.
In a **molten** compound, only its two ions are present. The metal forms at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode.
In an **aqueous** solution, water also supplies H⁺ and OH⁻, so there is a choice at each electrode.
At the cathode, the species with the more positive Eᶿ is reduced. Ions of metals below hydrogen, such as Cu²⁺ and Ag⁺, form the metal.
If the metal ion has a very negative Eᶿ, such as Na⁺ or Mg²⁺, then H₂ forms: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
At the anode, the species with the less positive Eᶿ is oxidised. In a dilute solution, oxygen forms: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.
In a **concentrated** halide solution, the halogen forms instead, for example 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻, because its high concentration makes it easier to discharge.
Reduction at the cathode, oxidation at the anode.
In aqueous solution, compare Eᶿ values and the concentration to decide the product.
Molten compounds give the metal at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode.

blocks.text: The charge on one mole of electrons is the Faraday constant, F. This section covers how to find it and the charge passed.

items.meaning: The charge carried by one mole of electrons. F = 96 500 C/mol.
The number of particles in one mole, 6.02 × 10²³ per mole.

blocks.label: Faraday constant
where: F is the Faraday constant in C/mol.
L is the Avogadro constant, 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
e is the charge on one electron, 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

blocks.label: Charge passed
where: Q is the charge in coulombs, C.
I is the current in amps, A.
t is the time in seconds, s.

items: F = Le, which is about 96 500 C/mol.
Q = It. Convert minutes to seconds first.

blocks.text: Every electrolysis calculation follows the same route from current and time to mass or volume.

items.text: Q = I × t, with t in seconds.
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu means 2 mol of e⁻ gives 1 mol of Cu. For 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻, 4 mol of e⁻ gives 1 mol of O₂.
Mass = moles × Ar or Mr. Gas volume = moles × 24 dm³/mol at room temperature and pressure.

diagram.alt: Practise finding the mass of copper deposited in electrolysis.
diagram.question: A current of **{i}** A passes through copper(II) sulfate solution for **{t}** seconds. Calculate the mass of copper deposited at the cathode in g. (F = 96 500 C/mol, Ar of Cu = 63.5)
working: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so moles of Cu = moles of electrons ÷ 2

items: Q = It, then moles of e⁻ = Q ÷ F, then use the half-equation.
Check the charge on the ion to find the electrons per atom.

blocks.text: The Avogadro constant can be found from an electrolysis experiment.

items.text: Use two clean, dried copper electrodes in copper(II) sulfate solution. Weigh the cathode.
Pass a constant current, measured with an ammeter, for a measured time.
Rinse, dry and reweigh the cathode. The increase in mass is the copper deposited.
Moles of Cu = mass ÷ 63.5. Moles of e⁻ = 2 × moles of Cu. F = Q ÷ moles of e⁻.
L = F ÷ e, with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

items: Keep the current constant, for example by adjusting a rheostat.
The anode loses mass. Its loss should match the gain at the cathode.
Measure the cathode's mass gain, the current and the time.
F = Q ÷ moles of e⁻, then L = F ÷ e.
